howto.build-deck.html:
🔗Build & Manage Decks

PLACEHOLDER: This page will be authored by Track C with verified content once the in-app docs surface (Track B4) ships. The structure below demonstrates the shell.

🔗Finding Cards

Use the search bar at the top of the Deck Builder to search by name. The results show only cards legal in the Edison format (March 2010 banlist). Each card displays its banlist status (Forbidden / Limited / Semi-Limited / Unlimited).

🔗Adding Cards

Tap or click a card to open its inspector, then use the + button to add it to your Main, Extra, or Side Deck. The builder enforces:

  • Main Deck: 40–60 cards
  • Extra Deck: 0–15 cards (Fusion + Synchro only)
  • Side Deck: 0–15 cards

🔗Legality Indicators

A chip at the top of the editor shows whether your deck is Valid or lists violations. Fix all violations before you can start a duel with that deck.

🔗Saving and Exporting

Your deck auto-saves as you edit. Use Export to download a .ydk file compatible with other simulators. Use Import to load a .ydk file.

meta.title: Getting Started
meta.summary: Create your account, accept an invite, and set up your profile to start playing Edison.

howto.getting-started.html:
🔗Getting Started

PLACEHOLDER: This page will be authored by Track C with verified content once the in-app docs surface (Track B4) ships. The structure below demonstrates the shell.

🔗Creating Your Account

You join the group via an invite link from an admin. Click the link, choose a display name, and set a password. Your account is ready immediately.

🔗Logging In

Go to the app URL and enter your display name and password. The app keeps you logged in for 30 days.

🔗What You Can Do

From Home you have three options:

  • Duel a friend — challenge another group member to a real-time duel
  • Build a deck — create and save Edison-format decks
  • Rules & Guides — this documentation section

meta.title: Ignition Effect Priority
meta.summary: After a Summon that did not start a chain, the turn player may activate an Ignition Effect as Chain Link 1 before the opponent can respond.

rules.diff.06.html:
🔗Rule #6 — Ignition Effect Priority

PLACEHOLDER: This page will be authored by Track C with verified content sourced from edisonformat.com once the in-app docs surface (Track B4) ships. The structure below demonstrates the intended article format.

TL;DR: On your turn, after a Summon that didn't start a chain, YOU may activate an Ignition Effect as Chain Link 1 before your opponent can respond (e.g. before Bottomless Trap Hole or Torrential Tribute).

🔗When the Summon Does NOT Start a Chain

Most Normal Summons and Special Summons do not start a chain by themselves. When this happens:

  1. The turn player (you) gets priority — the right to activate an Ignition Effect as Chain Link 1.
  2. You may use this to activate a monster's Ignition Effect immediately after the summon.
  3. Only after you pass priority (or activate an effect) can your opponent respond with a Trap card like Bottomless Trap Hole.

    4. Example: You Normal Summon Chaos Sorcerer. It does not start a chain. You invoke priority and banish a monster from your opponent's Graveyard with Chaos Sorcerer's Ignition Effect. Your opponent cannot activate Bottomless Trap Hole to respond to the Summon because the chain has already started.

    🔗When the Summon DOES Start a Chain

    Some monsters have Continuous, Trigger, or Flip Effects that activate automatically when Summoned, putting them on the chain. In this case:

    1. No priority window exists — the chain is already open.
    2. Your opponent may respond to that chain link normally.
    3. The turn player does not get a separate priority window for an Ignition Effect after the chain resolves.

      4. 🔗Related Cards

      Cards frequently involved in priority questions: Chaos Sorcerer, Sangan (Trigger, not Ignition), Brionac, Dragon of the Ice Barrier (Ignition).

meta.title: SEGOC — Simultaneous Effects Go on the Chain
meta.summary: When multiple effects trigger at the same time, they go on the chain in a fixed order: turn player's mandatory first, then turn player's optional, then opponent's mandatory, then opponent's optional.

rules.diff.07.html:
🔗Rule #7 — SEGOC

PLACEHOLDER: This page will be authored by Track C with verified content sourced from edisonformat.com once the in-app docs surface (Track B4) ships.

TL;DR: When multiple effects trigger simultaneously, they stack on the chain in a fixed order: turn player's mandatory effects → turn player's optional effects → opponent's mandatory effects → opponent's optional effects.

🔗The Four-Step SEGOC Order

When two or more Trigger Effects activate at the same time (e.g. two monsters die in the same chain resolution), they go on the chain in this exact sequence:

  1. Turn Player's Mandatory Triggers (Chain Link 1)
  2. Turn Player's Optional Triggers (Chain Link 2, if any)
  3. Non-Turn Player's Mandatory Triggers (Chain Link 3, if any)
  4. Non-Turn Player's Optional Triggers (Chain Link 4, if any)

    5. The chain then resolves in Last In, First Out (LIFO) order — the last effect added resolves first.

    🔗Why This Matters

    SEGOC determines who benefits from timing. An optional effect that ends up as the last Chain Link resolves first and cannot be negated by effects added earlier in the chain.

    Example: Your Sangan and your opponent's Sangan are both destroyed simultaneously. Your opponent is the turn player. The chain is: CL1 = opponent's Sangan (mandatory, turn player goes first even though it's optional — wait, Sangan is optional). See the full rule for how mandatory vs optional interacts.

    Note: The full SEGOC rule is nuanced. Track C will provide worked examples for each case.

meta.title: How a Turn Works
meta.summary: A turn has six phases: Draw, Standby, Main Phase 1, Battle Phase, Main Phase 2, End Phase. The first turn's player cannot attack.

rules.primer.turn.html:
🔗How a Turn Works

PLACEHOLDER: This page will be authored by Track C with verified content sourced from edisonformat.com once the in-app docs surface (Track B4) ships.

🔗Who Goes First

Before the duel begins, both players roll a die (or flip a coin). The winner chooses whether to go first or second. Going first has the advantage of setting up your board; going second lets you see what you're up against.

🔗Turn-1 Battle Phase Restriction

The player who goes first cannot conduct a Battle Phase on their first turn. This is a core Edison rule — you cannot attack on turn 1.

🔗The Six Phases

Each turn proceeds through these phases in order:

  1. Draw Phase (DP) — Draw one card from your Deck.
  2. Standby Phase (SP) — Mandatory effects that trigger "during the Standby Phase" activate here.
  3. Main Phase 1 (MP1) — Normal Summon, Set, activate Spells/Traps, use effects.
  4. Battle Phase (BP) — Declare attacks. Skipped on the first player's first turn.
  5. Main Phase 2 (MP2) — Like MP1; you may Normal Summon again only if you didn't in MP1.
  6. End Phase (EP) — Discard to the hand limit (6 cards) and resolve end-of-turn effects.

    7. 🔗Priority and the Turn Player

    The turn player acts first in each phase. See Rule #6 (Ignition Effect Priority) for the specific rules about when each player can activate effects.
